newsitem.title: USA: IMF upbeat on world inflation developments.
newsitem.headline: IMF upbeat on world inflation developments.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday painted an optimistic picture of inflation developments in countries around the world but stressed the need for continued vigilance against price pressures.
"Inflation rates in industrial countries, as well as in a number of developing countries, have declined to their lowest levels in decades," the Fund said in its semi-annual "World Economic Outlook."
The report said that in a number of industrial countries, inflation rates are "close to, or approaching, reasonable price stability."
However, the IMF cautioned, "Monetary authorities will, of course, need to remain vigilant to incipient price pressures as growth continues or strengthens."

"With appropriately designed monetary and fiscal policies, it should be possible to keep inflation low and to reduce it further over time, while minimizing undesirable short-term fluctuations in output," the IMF said.

On the subject of working toward price stability while minimizing adverse consequences for economic output, the IMF report made reference to a monetary policy approach called "opportunistic disinflation," which was outlined in a recent study by two Federal Reserve Board economists. The approach takes advantage of recessions to achieve gains against inflation.

"The U.S. Federal Reserve in particular has emphasized the importance of preventing inflation from rising significantly during economic expansions while taking advantage of economic slowdowns to bring inflation down," the IMF said.
Looking at the reasons for the favorable inflation developments, the Fund gave credit to central banks and governments for their determination to bring prices under control.

"Despite initial hesitation and policy mistakes, governments and central banks have applied the hard-learned lessons from the high inflation decades of the 1970s and 1980s with increasing success," the Fund said.
The IMF also said increased openness to trade has also played a role in tempering inflation.
While emphasizing the importance of working toward price stability, the report suggested that a zero inflation rate may not be an optimal target for central banks.
It pointed out that perceived upward baises in the inflation gauges of many countries could mean that they might run the risk of deflation if they were to target zero inflation.
The report also highlighted the difficulty of engineering negative real short-term interest rates, if needed in times of recession, when inflation is zero.

On the other hand, the Fund pointed to benefits for growth from low inflation, saying, "The evidence is strongly indicative of a negative relationship between inflation and long-term growth, even at moderates rates of inflation of 10 to 30 percent."
"High rates of inflation are clearly harmful to growth," the Fund said.
